To avoid like the plague means to stay away from someone or something as completely and strongly as possible. Not just a little bit — but totally, deliberately, and with great effort.

When you use this idiom, you're saying that your avoidance is extreme. You don't just prefer not to be near something — you want absolutely nothing to do with it.

Think of it this way: if someone offers you food you hate and you say "No thanks," that's normal avoidance. But if you walk out of the room the moment it appears, that's avoiding it like the plague.

To truly understand this idiom, you need to understand the word plague — specifically, the Bubonic Plague, also known as the Black Death.

The Bubonic Plague was one of the most terrifying diseases in all of human history. In the 14th century (around 1347–1351), it swept across Europe and Asia and killed roughly one-third of Europe's entire population — that's tens of millions of people. It spread rapidly, it was incredibly painful, and at the time, it was almost always fatal.

Here's the key part: there was no cure. No medicine, no treatment, no doctor could save you. The only strategy anyone had was to run away. If you heard the plague was in a nearby town, you fled. If a person in your house got sick, you got as far away from them as possible. Staying near an infected person meant you would almost certainly die too.

So people didn't just "avoid" the plague — they avoided it with absolute, desperate, life-or-death urgency.

Over time, this extreme behavior entered the English language as a way to describe any very strong avoidance. The idiom has been in use in English for several centuries, with written records tracing it back to at least the 1500s. It basically asks: "How do you avoid something? The same way people once avoided the plague — completely and without hesitation."

The idiom follows a simple, flexible structure:

[Subject] + avoid + [person/thing] + like the plague

You slot in whatever is being avoided in the middle. That's it.

Here are a variety of examples so you can see it used in real contexts:

About a person:

  • "Ever since he started lying to everyone, his colleagues avoid him like the plague."
  • "She used to be my friend, but after our fight, she avoids me like the plague."

About a place:

  • "That restaurant gave me food poisoning twice. I avoid it like the plague now."
  • "He avoids the gym like the plague — he hasn't exercised in years."

About a topic or situation:

  • "My father avoids any conversation about money like the plague."
  • "She avoids confrontation like the plague and will do anything to keep the peace."

About a thing:

  • "I avoid spicy food like the plague — my stomach can't handle it."
  • "He avoids social media like the plague and says it just makes him anxious."

Notice that it works for people, places, situations, topics, and objects. It is very flexible.

The idiom carries a sense of strong negative emotion toward whatever is being avoided. That emotion could be:

  • Disgust — "I avoid that type of music like the plague."
  • Fear — "She avoids hospitals like the plague."
  • Annoyance — "He avoids meetings like the plague."
  • Bad past experience — "After that disaster, I avoid that road like the plague."

The reason for the avoidance doesn't have to be life-threatening. The idiom is used hyperbolically — meaning it exaggerates the intensity of avoidance for effect, just like saying "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse" doesn't mean you'll actually eat a horse. You're using dramatic language to make a point strongly.
Tone and Register — When to Use It

This is an informal idiom. You'll hear it in:

  • Everyday casual conversation
  • Informal writing (texts, social media posts, blogs, personal emails)
  • Humorous or light-hearted contexts

You would generally not use it in:

  • Formal essays or academic writing
  • Professional business reports
  • Official documents

However, it can appear in informal workplace conversations or casual emails between colleagues who know each other well.

A few things to be clear about:

  • It does not mean avoiding something only sometimes or occasionally. The avoidance it describes is consistent and absolute.
  • It does not require a literal health reason. The thing being avoided doesn't have to be dangerous or harmful in reality — it just has to be something the speaker strongly dislikes or wants nothing to do with.
  • It does not imply that the speaker is afraid, specifically. It might be fear, but it could just as easily be strong dislike, annoyance, or past bad experience.

These idioms and phrases have a similar meaning and are useful to know alongside this one:

  • "Steer clear of" — "Steer clear of that guy; he always causes drama."
  • "Give something/someone a wide berth" — "I give that topic a wide berth in conversations with her." (This comes from sailing — you sail far away from a dangerous obstacle.)
  • "Keep at arm's length" — "She keeps her coworkers at arm's length and doesn't share personal information." (This one has a slightly different shade — it means maintaining emotional or social distance, not always complete physical avoidance.)
  • "Want nothing to do with" — "After that experience, I want nothing to do with that company."

None of these are exact synonyms, but they all describe the idea of deliberate distancing from something.

QuestionAnswer

What does it mean? To avoid someone or something completely, extremely, and deliberately.

Where does it come from? The Bubonic Plague of the 14th century, when fleeing infected people was the only way to survive.

Is the avoidance literal? No — it's exaggerated for effect. The thing doesn't have to be actually dangerous.

Who or what can be avoided? Anything — people, places, situations, topics, foods, activities.

What tone does it carry? Informal, often with a touch of humor or drama.

The beauty of this idiom is that it borrows the weight of one of history's greatest tragedies to describe something as simple as not liking your neighbor or hating a type of food. That contrast between the dramatic origin and the everyday usage is exactly what gives the idiom its punchy, memorable character.
